tagline: A railroad bypass left Piedmont behind, with its charcoal kilns surviving.
intro: Muddy Creek Historic Backway connects Fort Bridger, Muddy Creek and the ghost town of Piedmont by back roads. The Wyoming Office of Tourism describes a 25-mile historic route centered on western migration, with a former campsite and surviving charcoal kilns. Its branching route includes a return leg from Piedmont to the junction leading toward I-80 Exit 24.

Water and tall bunchgrass made Muddy Creek a campsite for westward travelers and their animals. The transcontinental railroad passed through in 1869. At Piedmont, helper engines needed wood and water to work a steep railroad grade, bringing railroad families into town. Later, the Aspen tunnel eliminated that winding climb; the new line bypassed Piedmont by several miles, and the town declined.

For an eastbound journey, begin with Piedmont and its sandstone kilns, then retrace the branch north before turning east toward Fort Bridger. Muddy Creek marks the corridor used by emigrant companies, a stage stop and a Pony Express station. Finish in Fort Bridger, where the historic site includes a reconstructed trading post.

moments.title: Piedmont Charcoal Kilns
moments.text: Three beehive-shaped sandstone kilns survive at Piedmont. Moses Byrne built five here; two have since been destroyed. Most of his charcoal went to small smelters and blacksmith shops in the Salt Lake Valley. The surviving kilns have walls 24 inches thick and rise about 30 feet. They entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1971 and are managed by Wyoming as a state historic site. Byrne also built Pony Express stations and stables.
moments.notice: Look for the three beehive-shaped kilns built from local sandstone.

moments.title: Muddy Creek
moments.text: Good water and tall bunchgrass made this a useful place to feed animals during westward journeys. Brigham Young's first group of Mormon pioneers used Muddy Creek in the summer of 1847. In June 1858, 2,000 U.S. Army men camped here. The site also held the Muddy Overland Stage Stop and a Pony Express station. In 1869, the original transcontinental railroad bed passed through.

moments.title: Fort Bridger
moments.text: The trading post at Fort Bridger is a reconstruction. The original establishment of Jim Bridger and Louis Vasquez supplied travelers on the Oregon Trail and served as a trading place with local Native Americans. Its modest arrangement consisted of two log cabins connected by a fence that held horses. Travelers also used its blacksmith shop. By 1858, the fort had become a military outpost. The historic site now includes the reconstructed trading post and a museum.
